nameStory: This tiny moss gets its 'capillary' name from its thread-like leaves that are as fine as human hair - capillary comes from the Latin word for hair. The 'thread-moss' part describes how the narrow leaves create a delicate, stringy appearance when you look closely with a hand lens.
description: Capillary Thread-moss is a small, cushion-forming moss that creates soft, bright green patches on soil and rocks. Individual plants are tiny - usually less than half an inch tall - but they often grow together in dense colonies that can spread several inches across. When dry, the patches turn yellowish-green and look almost brittle, but they spring back to vibrant green when moistened.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely narrow, thread-like leaves that feel soft and delicate to the touch - think of the finest embroidery thread

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, dense cushions or low tufts that feel springy when gently pressed with your finger

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright emerald green when wet, shifting to pale yellowish-green when dry - the color change is quite dramatic

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small, oval capsules on thin stalks in late spring - the capsules dangle like tiny lanterns

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels velvety soft when moist but becomes crispy and fragile when completely dry

habitat: Look for Capillary Thread-moss on disturbed soil, clay banks, and bare patches in gardens, along trails, and near stream banks throughout New England. It particularly loves slightly acidic soil and often appears after soil has been turned over or eroded. You'll also find it growing on old brick walls and in the cracks of concrete walkways.

seasonality.spring: Most visible and vibrant green as snow melts and spring rains keep it hydrated. Sporophytes with tiny capsules typically develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: May become less noticeable during dry spells when it turns pale and shrinks, but look for it in consistently moist, shaded spots.
seasonality.fall: Returns to bright green with autumn rains and becomes quite prominent again on bare soil and disturbed ground.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often hidden under snow; on mild winter days, you can find bright green patches on south-facing banks.

funFact: This moss can lose up to 95% of its water content and appear completely dead, then fully revive within minutes of getting wet - it's like having a resurrection superpower that works hundreds of times throughout its life!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small thread-mosses, but Capillary Thread-moss has the narrowest leaves of the group - if the leaves look thick enough to be called 'stringy' rather than 'hair-like,' you're probably looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: Identification confidence is moderate due to limited reference material for this species. The moss family contains many similar-looking species that require microscopic examination for certain identification.**
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Long-leaved Thread Moss, Capillary Thread-moss has much finer, more delicate leaves that truly look hair-thin rather than string-like. Tufted Thread-moss forms more compact, dome-shaped cushions, while Capillary Thread-moss tends to spread in looser patches with a more relaxed growth pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Capillary Thread-moss which prefers disturbed soils, Long-leaved Thread Moss sticks to natural wetlands.
Compared to its relatives like Long-leaved Thread Moss, this species forms much more compact, dense cushions rather than loose tufts.
Compared to Long-leaved Thread Moss, this species has shorter, more overlapping leaves and forms tighter cushions rather than loose mats.
